Cushioned play surfaces on Edgewood's mid-century lots

Edgewood's own landscaping code caps grass height at 12 inches as a nuisance rule, a line a play surface never approaches since it never grows at all. A cushioned play area installed here costs $10–$25 a square foot as of September 2026, with the shock pad matched to the specific equipment's fall height rather than a flat guess.

Reviewed by Luis Austin, owner · Last reviewed September 21, 2026

A code written for mowing, and a surface that skips it entirely

Edgewood's Chapter 114 treats grass taller than 12 inches as a code violation, a rule aimed at mowing compliance on living lawns rather than at play surfaces specifically (Chapter 114, Municode). A synthetic play area never grows past that line in the first place, which sidesteps the nuisance question entirely, though the state's own turf standard, not the city's mowing rule, is still what governs the pad, backing and infill underneath the equipment.

Fitting a play corner into a smaller Edgewood backyard

With roughly 2,700 residents on lots that run smaller than the ranch-era acreage found a few miles east, an Edgewood play area typically claims one defined corner of the yard rather than spreading across it, leaving room for a family's regular lawn on the same property (Edgewood, Florida). Containment edging around that corner matters for one specific reason: it's what keeps rubber infill from migrating past the footprint Florida's rule actually permits it in, which is strictly the ground directly under the equipment.

Grading a play area's base toward a drainage point

A Edgewood play surface's base carries the same one to two percent grade toward a drainage point that any residential lawn does, compacted in lifts before the shock pad goes down on top. That slope matters more here than it does under grass, since a shock pad sitting in standing water softens and loses cushioning performance faster than a lawn's backing degrades from the same exposure. Getting the grade right under the rock, before the pad and turf ever go down, is what keeps the finished play surface draining the way it's designed to for years rather than months.

The final walk-through before handing off a play surface

The last step on a Edgewood playground project is infilling at the manufacturer's specified rate, then walking the finished surface to check for flat, even coverage and confirm nothing shifted during the last stages of the build. This walk-through is where a crew catches a low spot, an uneven seam, or a containment edge that needs a final adjustment before calling the job finished. Skipping this check and assuming a play surface is ready just because the visible steps are done is how small problems make it to the first day of use instead of getting caught beforehand.

Say you have a 300 sq ft play corner near Orange Avenue

A 300 square foot play corner behind an Edgewood home a few streets off Orange Avenue, sized for a swing set and a slide, prices between $3,600 and $5,700 at the published $12–$19 typical range, with the shock pad's thickness set by the equipment's tallest fall height rather than a flat guess. Because the lot itself runs on the smaller side, that 300 square feet often sits close to a fence line on at least one edge, which affects how the containment border gets anchored more than it affects the price. The rest of the yard's lawn, if any remains once the play corner and any dog run are laid out, prices separately at the residential range.

What ASTM F1292 actually tests

ASTM F1292 is the standard test method behind any shock pad's fall-height rating, measuring how much a surfacing product cushions an impact within a playground's use zone rather than just how thick or soft the material feels by hand. A Edgewood homeowner or daycare operator comparing two pad products should ask for the F1292 test data behind each one's claimed rating, since two pads that look and feel similar can carry different tested fall-height numbers depending on their internal construction. The rating on a spec sheet is only as good as the test data supporting it.

Low ground near the lakes and what it means for the base

The flatwoods sand common around Edgewood's two lakes, mapped to Basinger and Immokalee series soils, holds a seasonal high water table closer to the surface than the drier ridge ground found toward Conway to the east (Basinger series description; Immokalee series description). A play area's shock pad needs to drain at least as fast as that base moves water, which is part of why the crushed-rock layer underneath gets built toward the fuller end of the state's allowed depth on a lot near either lake.

Our article on turf safety for kids covers the PFAS and infill questions parents ask most, and the playground turf guide goes through ASTM fall-height ratings in full. The Edgewood turf guide above has the lot-size context; Pine Castle and Oak Ridge handle similar small-lot play areas nearby.

The temperature jump between a play surface and the patio beside it

A Edgewood play area built right next to a bare concrete patio creates a temperature contrast worth planning for, since turf in full sun reaches 120 to 150°F while unshaded concrete nearby can run even hotter, meaning a child crossing from a rinsed play surface onto that patio edge can meet a worse surface than the one they just left rather than a cooler one. Rinsing the patio border along with the turf before playtime addresses both surfaces at once rather than assuming the padded turf side was the only one that needed attention. This matters most at the exact meeting point where the two surfaces touch.

What to record about a play surface at handoff

On the day a Edgewood play area is finished, writing down the shock pad's brand and rated fall height alongside the exact equipment height it was matched to pays off later, since that record is what makes a future recheck possible if the equipment ever gets replaced with something taller. Without it, confirming years later whether an aging pad still covers a new piece of equipment means tracking down old paperwork or guessing, neither of which a parent wants to do quickly. A photo of the pad's spec label before turf goes over it, kept with other home records, solves this in under a minute on install day.

Questions people ask

Does Edgewood's 12-inch grass rule apply to playground turf?

No. That nuisance rule targets mowing on living lawns, and a synthetic play surface never grows tall enough to trigger it. The surface still has to meet the state's own material and shock-pad standards regardless.

Why does a play area near Edgewood's lakes need a deeper base than one further inland?

The Basinger and Immokalee soils common around Lake Jessamine and Lake Mary Jess hold water closer to the surface than drier ground a few miles away, so building the crushed-rock base toward the fuller end of the state's allowed depth keeps the shock pad draining at the rate it needs to.
